payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Low Water Year
by Teodora Hallsey
The following passage is from the novel The Low Water Year (1957) by Teodora Hallsey. Agnes, nineteen, has been sent from the mainland to the island where her grandmother once lived.

```passage
    The ferry put Agnes off at Scarrow at eleven, and
she walked up from the slip with her grandmother's house
key in one glove and the bill of sale, already made out,
in the other. She had been told not to go up to the
house. "There is nothing in it you want," Hedda had said
from the bed in the mainland home, "and if you go in you
will start wanting." So Agnes turned left along the
shingle toward the boat shed instead, in city shoes, the
stones rolling under her like something that had not
agreed to be walked on.

    The Linnet lay keel-down on her cradle where she had
been hauled in October, and she looked smaller than
Agnes remembered, the way the island did, the way the
dock did; only the sky had kept its size. Someone had
put a tarpaulin over her and weighted it with four
stones, one at each corner, exactly. Agnes knew who. Osk
Pell did everything in fours. He came down the path from
his own place while she was still working the first
stone loose, and he did not help her, and he did not
hurry.

    "You'll be Hedda's girl," he said. He was a square,
slow, salt-cured man with a face the weather had been at
for sixty years and had not finished. "She wrote me you
were coming. She wrote me what to pay." "She told me not
to argue the price." "There isn't a price to argue." He
named it. It was less than her train fare had been.
Agnes looked at the hull, at the strake her grandfather
had replaced the summer she was nine, the new wood still
a shade paler, like a scar that had decided to stay.
"That boat is worth ten times that," she said. "You know
it is." "I know it is."

    She had come to do a plain thing. You sold a boat;
you took the money; you caught the four o'clock back.
Now the plain thing had a hole in it and she could feel
the cold coming through. She remembered Hedda in the
stern with the tiller under her arm like a parcel she
had no intention of giving up, not steering so much as
declining to let the boat go anywhere else. She
remembered Osk Pell on the dock those summers, never
once in the boat. Never once.

    "Your grandfather owed me for the engine," Pell
said. "Nineteen thirty-eight. He never paid it and I
never asked, and your grandmother never forgot it.
That's the price. She's paying the debt. She wants it to
look like a sale." He took the stones off the other
three corners himself now, one, two, three, setting each
on the shingle as if it might be needed again. "If I'd
offered her a fair price she'd have refused it. She'd
have let the boat rot sooner than take money from me."

    Agnes thought of the coin you were supposed to put
in the mouth of the dead for the ferryman, and how the
stories never said what happened if the ferryman was the
one who paid. Across the water the mainland was a gray
line with the home somewhere on it, a window, a bed, a
woman who had arranged the whole morning from under a
blanket and sent her granddaughter to stand in the wind
and be the hands of it. Agnes had thought she was the
one doing the selling. She signed the bill of sale on
the Linnet's gunwale, pressing hard so the pencil would
take on the damp paper, and Pell counted the money into
her glove, and it was so little that it did not change
the shape of her hand.

    "Go up to the house," Pell said. "She told you not
to. Go anyway. There's a bailer in the kitchen she took
off the boat so I wouldn't get it. It's got her initials
in it. Take it to her." Agnes did not answer. She walked
back along the shingle, and the stones rolled the same
as before, but she had the time now to let them, and at
the turn where the path went up to the house instead of
down to the slip, she stood for a while and let the four
o'clock leave without her.
```

provenance.note: Original passage written for practice purposes; invented author, title, island and characters.

characters: Agnes Rune, nineteen, raised partly on the island, now living on the mainland; sent by her grandmother to sell the family boat
Hedda Rune, Agnes's grandmother, bedridden in a mainland home, absent from the scene but directing it by letter
Osk Pell, an island neighbor in his sixties, buyer of the boat, former creditor of Agnes's grandfather
blueprint.setting: Scarrow Island, a small northern fishing island reached by ferry, late autumn in the 1950s; the shingle beach, the boat shed, the hauled-out boat Linnet; the mainland visible as a gray line across the water
blueprint.situation: Agnes arrives on the morning ferry with a pre-written bill of sale and instructions not to haggle and not to go up to the house. Pell names an absurdly low price, then reveals that Hedda set it herself to repay an old debt disguised as a sale.
blueprint.conflict: Agnes believes she is performing a plain transaction on her own authority; she discovers she is the instrument of her grandmother's arrangement with Pell, and must decide whether to obey the instruction to stay away from the house and catch the afternoon ferry.
blueprint.central_idea: Acts of settling accounts between the old are carried out through the young, who discover that what looked like their own errand was someone else's unfinished business; the recognition of being used is also a recognition of belonging.
blueprint.complexity: Hedda's manipulation is both a humiliation of Agnes and a kind of trust; Pell's acceptance of an unfair price in his favor is also an act of loyalty to a dead man and a proud woman; Agnes's final disobedience (going up to the house, missing the ferry) is simultaneously a rejection of being used and a deeper acceptance of her place in the family's accounts. The boat, sold for nothing, is worth more to everyone than its price.

devices.quote: like something that had not agreed to be walked on
devices.function: Figures the island shingle as resisting Agnes's return, establishing her estrangement and the island's indifference to her errand

devices.quote: like a scar that had decided to stay
devices.function: The replaced plank becomes a healed wound with its own will, tying the boat to family history and to the stubbornness that governs the sale

devices.quote: a face the weather had been at for sixty years
devices.function: Weather becomes an unfinished craftsman working on Pell, marking him as shaped by the island and suggesting incompleteness, the way the debt is unfinished

devices.quote: the plain thing had a hole in it
devices.function: Agnes's simple plan is figured as a leaking hull, letting cold in; links her inner disturbance to the boat and foreshadows the bailer

devices.quote: You sold a boat; you took the money
devices.function: Agnes's brisk mental script in second-person generalities exposes her wish for the errand to be impersonal, which the scene denies

devices.quote: She remembered Hedda in the stern
devices.function: Inserts the image of Hedda refusing to let the boat go anywhere before Pell explains the price, so his explanation confirms rather than surprises

devices.quote: the coin you were supposed to put in the mouth of the dead
devices.function: Charon's fee frames the sale as a passage toward death and the money as funeral payment; the inversion (the ferryman paying) captures Agnes's confusion about who is giving and who is taking

devices.quote: She wants it to look like a sale.
devices.function: The sale that Agnes came to perform is revealed as a disguise for a repayment, undercutting the title act of the passage

devices.quote: it did not change the shape of her hand
devices.function: The money's triviality is registered physically rather than announced, flattening the climax into a wry, bodily fact
Compressed sibilants give Pell a solid, deliberate sound matching his unhurried conduct
The fragment insists on Pell's lifelong exclusion from the boat, hinting at the unpaid debt before it is spoken

devices.quote: There's a bailer in the kitchen
devices.function: The bailer Hedda removed so Pell would not get it symbolizes what she withholds even while giving; carrying it to her becomes the task Agnes chooses over the one assigned

devices.quote: he did not help her, and he did not hurry
devices.function: Pell's deliberateness against Agnes's haste in city shoes defines her as the outsider and him as the island's tempo

devices.quote: Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
devices.function: The sentence turns from brisk transaction to rueful recognition of being used, redirecting the passage toward Agnes's choice

devices.quote: the stones rolled the same as before
devices.function: Returns the opening image with Agnes's altered relation to it: the ground has not changed, her hurry has

devices.quote: There isn't a price to argue.
devices.function: Pell's flat refusal to bargain signals that the transaction is not economic, before he explains why

shifts.quote: Agnes had thought she was the one doing the selling.
shifts.from: Agnes as brisk agent of a plain transaction
shifts.to: Agnes as instrument of her grandmother's arrangement, rueful and newly aware

shifts.quote: let the four o'clock leave without her
shifts.from: Compliance with Hedda's instructions and the plan to leave
shifts.to: Deliberate disobedience and lingering, accepting the island's slower time

blueprint.speaker: Third-person limited narrator aligned with Agnes; access to her memories and thoughts but not Pell's or Hedda's
blueprint.form_notes: Seven paragraphs of prose; clipped dialogue; one flashback paragraph; closing paragraph returns to the opening shingle image.

items.stem: A student claims that Hedda controls the sale despite her absence from the island. Which of the following sentences of commentary most clearly links the phrase "arranged the whole morning from under a blanket" (lines 55-56) to that claim?

options.text: The sentence shows that Agnes resents being sent into the wind, which establishes the conflict between the two generations of the family.
options.why: Shifts focus from Hedda's control to Agnes's resentment and generational conflict, which the quoted phrase does not itself address.
options.label: wrong_scope

options.text: The sentence describes Hedda lying in bed at the home, which proves she is too ill to travel to the island herself to sell the boat.
options.why: Explains Hedda's absence rather than her control; it restates the circumstance without connecting to the claim's main point.
options.label: wrong_function

options.text: The sentence pairs a verb of command with an image of confinement, showing that Hedda's authority survives the loss of her mobility.
options.why: Directly connects the evidence ('arranged' against 'under a blanket') to the claim about control despite absence; the passage supports it with Hedda's letters to Pell and instructions to Agnes.
options.label: correct

options.text: The sentence uses the word 'blanket' to suggest that Hedda is hiding something from Agnes, which the reader learns is the debt owed to Pell.
options.why: Over-reads 'blanket' as concealment; the text uses it for physical confinement, and the hidden debt is Pell's revelation, not the point of this phrase.
options.label: lexical_trap

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "dryly understated, registering the sum's insignificance as a bodily fact". Rather than naming anger or disappointment, the narrator measures the money by what it fails to do to a glove, a restrained wryness characteristic of the whole passage.
"bitter, as Agnes openly condemns Pell for exploiting her grandmother's pride" is incorrect: The sentence is flat and physical, not condemnatory; Agnes has already learned that Pell's price was Hedda's design.
"tender, as Agnes recognizes the money as a token of Pell's love for her family" is incorrect: The passage does not frame the money as a token of love, and Agnes's response is withholding, not tender.
"triumphant, as Agnes realizes the boat has been kept from the open market" is incorrect: There is no triumph; Agnes has just recognized she was used, and the sentence deflates rather than elevates.

items.stem: Which of the following thesis statements offers the most defensible and specific interpretation of the passage?

options.text: Through the recurring image of the shingle and Agnes's silence at the end, the passage shows that she becomes the instrument of an old debt and, in resisting that role, discovers a claim on the island.
options.why: Names specific techniques (recurring image, final silence) and a complex idea with tension (used, yet discovering belonging), both grounded in the text's opening and closing.
options.label: correct

options.text: Through the description of the boat and the island, the passage shows that Agnes travels to Scarrow, sells the Linnet to Pell for a small sum, and then misses the afternoon ferry.
options.why: Summarizes plot rather than interpreting it; no claim about meaning or complexity is made.
options.label: wrong_function

options.text: Through Pell's dialogue and Hedda's letters, the passage shows that older people often manipulate the young, and that such manipulation is always harmful to family relationships.
options.why: Generalizes beyond the text to 'older people' and 'always harmful'; the passage treats Hedda's arrangement with more ambivalence.
options.label: too_broad

options.text: Through the allusion to the ferryman and the sale's low price, the passage shows that Pell is the true owner of the boat and that Agnes comes to accept his superior moral claim to it.
options.why: The text never asserts Pell's ownership or moral superiority, and Agnes's final silence toward him does not signal acceptance of such a claim.
options.label: unsupported

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Through the recurring image of the shingle and Agnes's silence at the end, the passage shows that she becomes the instrument of an old debt and, in resisting that role, discovers a claim on the island.". Names specific techniques (recurring image, final silence) and a complex idea with tension (used, yet discovering belonging), both grounded in the text's opening and closing.
"Through the description of the boat and the island, the passage shows that Agnes travels to Scarrow, sells the Linnet to Pell for a small sum, and then misses the afternoon ferry." is incorrect: Summarizes plot rather than interpreting it; no claim about meaning or complexity is made.
"Through Pell's dialogue and Hedda's letters, the passage shows that older people often manipulate the young, and that such manipulation is always harmful to family relationships." is incorrect: Generalizes beyond the text to 'older people' and 'always harmful'; the passage treats Hedda's arrangement with more ambivalence.
"Through the allusion to the ferryman and the sale's low price, the passage shows that Pell is the true owner of the boat and that Agnes comes to accept his superior moral claim to it." is incorrect: The text never asserts Pell's ownership or moral superiority, and Agnes's final silence toward him does not signal acceptance of such a claim.

review_notes.key_flaw: 'In resisting that role' is debatable. Agnes heads toward the house because Pell tells her to, and her purpose is to take the bailer to Hedda, which arguably continues her role as the family's go-between. Her 'silence' is a single 'did not answer.'
